analysis.body:
Federal agencies are in the early stages of deploying AI, with significant capability but uneven execution. According to the GAO, twenty of twenty-three major agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned artificial intelligence use cases, yet most of these remain in the planning phase rather than production. The GAO found that in about 200 instances agencies reported currently using AI operationally, with specific applications including analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing photographs from drones, and targeting of scientific specimens for planetary rovers. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of AI use cases among federal agencies inventoried.

The government's capacity to manage AI adoption is constrained by incomplete frameworks and inconsistent implementation. The GAO documented that five of twenty agencies provided comprehensive information for each reported use case, while fifteen had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data, with some inventories omitting required elements such as the AI life cycle stage or releasability status. The office found that ten of twenty-three agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, twelve implemented some but not all, and one was exempt from requirements. Critical gaps remain: OMB has not yet developed government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI, and OPM has not established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work, meaning agencies cannot consistently manage AI deployment.

Recognition of AI's potential is pushing investment and policy attention upward. The President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI, signaling federal commitment despite implementation challenges. Across the international landscape, the OECD.AI Policy Observatory tracks over 900 national AI policies and initiatives and has moved to integrate government AI work under a unified GPAI framework focused on helping AI actors develop trustworthy systems that respect human rights and are fair, transparent, explainable, robust, secure and safe.

Legislative activity on AI governance is accelerating at the state level, with 5,915 AI bills tracked across all fifty-three U.S. jurisdictions as of the latest update. This proliferation reflects mounting concern about regulation, but also fragmentation: without federal acquisition guidance or occupational standards, state-level regulation risks creating compliance complexity for agencies operating across borders.

Stanford HAI's AI Index identifies a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared governments are to manage it, even as technical capabilities improve and adoption spreads. The index notes that frameworks needed to govern, evaluate, and understand the technology are falling behind, particularly in data transparency where the field shows declining openness. For a government entity considering AI deployment, the evidence suggests the technology can deliver operational gains in data analysis and imaging tasks, but success depends heavily on completing basic inventory and governance requirements first—agencies without comprehensive inventories and clear lifecycle tracking have hindered their own management capacity and risk exposure.

https://oecd.ai/.brief: OECD.AI is a policy observatory that maintains a database of over 900 national AI policies and initiatives, alongside live AI data and policy analysis. The platform promotes the OECD AI Principles to help countries develop trustworthy AI systems, and invites organisations developing advanced AI to submit reports on their risk mitigation measures to improve transparency and comparability. In July 2024, the GPAI initiative merged with OECD member countries' AI work under the GPAI brand to form an integrated partnership. The observatory aims to support AI actors in building systems that respect human rights, fairness, transparency, explainability, robustness, and security.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-laws/.brief: The page lists AI laws by state, noting that LegiScan tracks 5,915 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, updated daily. It also advertises books by Stephen R. Jordan, including the “Operating Discipline for AI Library™” series, now available on Amazon. In addition, the page enumerates a series of AI audit and assessment services such as the AI Business Enablement Audit, AI Readiness & Performance Assessment, AI Risk & Governance Review, AI Efficiency & Process Optimization, AI IT Security Audit, AI IT Security Implementation & Strategy, Secure by Design in the Age of AI, Application Security in the Age of AI, and The AI Lawyer. The content is presented as a list of resources and services related to AI legislation and compliance.

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-1059.brief: GAO reported that federal agencies have begun implementing AI, which is defined as computing systems that “learn” how to improve their performance, but many policy requirements remain unmet. Twenty of 23 agencies listed about 1,200 AI use cases, most still in planning and only roughly 200 in production, and inventories often omitted required data such as life-cycle stage or releasability. While Commerce and the GSA fully met selected requirements, agencies like OMB, OPM, and OSTP did not, and only ten agencies met all their AI requirements, twelve met some, and one was exempt. The report notes that AI can improve government operations but also poses risks, and the FY 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for non-defense AI R&D.
